sources.title: Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs: The history of Switzerland
sources.note: Old Confederation, French invasion in 1798, Mediation, 1815 settlement, Sonderbund War and federal constitution of 1848.

sources.title: Swiss Federal Archives: Epoche des Wandels, 1798 to 1848
sources.note: 1798 Helvetic constitution, 1803 Mediation and 1815 Federal Treaty; distinguishes successive constitutional arrangements.

sources.title: Swiss National Museum: From cottage industries to the home office
sources.note: Appenzell weaving cellars; merchant-supplied materials and looms; family labor; regional linen and cotton production.

sources.title: University of Basel: Historical timeline
sources.note: 1529 interruption, 1531 anatomical dissection, 1532 reopening, 1533 scholarships and 1538 Erasmus Foundation.

sources.title: University of Basel: Erasmus and the New Testament exhibition
sources.note: Exhibition cases on Novum Instrumentum / Novum Testamentum editions, 1516 to 1535; manuscripts, Greek text and Latin scholarship.

sources.title: Stapfer Enquête research project: Die Stapfer-Enquête
sources.note: 1799 questionnaire of about 60 questions, over 2,400 school responses, overwhelmingly from teachers; four thematic groups.

sources.title: Swiss National Museum: When children toiled in factories
sources.note: 1877 federal factory legislation; invented opening characters are not used. Historical Gubel institution and contemporary reports are distinguished from illustrative fiction.

sources.title: Swiss National Museum: The food on the working man’s table
sources.note: Industrial food production, Maggi factory image dated 1910, Daniel Peter’s milk chocolate and Lindt’s conching in 1879.

sources.title: Swiss National Museum: The bidet, furniture designed for cleansing
sources.note: Specific Jegenstorf Castle mahogany bidet, second half of nineteenth century; removable ceramic bowl and cover. Generalizations about universal bathing customs are not adopted.

sources.title: Swiss Parliament: Frauen stimmen
sources.note: Federal women’s suffrage 1971; Appenzell Innerrhoden required by Federal Court in 1990, first cantonal participation 1991.

sources.title: Swiss Parliament documentation: equality and women’s suffrage
sources.note: Indexed extract directly quotes 1848 constitution article 4 and explains exclusion of women from political equality; quotation checked against primary transcription at verfassungen.ch/verf48.htm.

sources.title: University of Basel: Translating the Bible
sources.note: Erasmus’s philological work using Greek manuscripts including material brought from Byzantium by John of Ragusa.

sources.title: Belgian government: Provisional government and National Congress
sources.note: 1830 independence and elected National Congress; constitution 7 February 1831.

sources.title: Belgian government: Formation of the federal state
sources.note: Successive language laws and constitutional reforms; formally federal state in 1993.

sources.title: Belgian Senate: Constitution belge, 7 February 1831
sources.note: Original constitution transcription, article 25; do not confuse its numbering with current article 33.

sources.title: Belgian Senate: Parliamentary elections since 1831
sources.note: Property-based franchise, plural male voting, one male vote after 1919 and women’s national franchise from 1948.

sources.title: Belgian Senate: Universal suffrage and women, article 5/6
sources.note: Law 27 March 1948; first national election with women voters 26 June 1949.

sources.title: Train World: België op het spoor, nineteenth century
sources.note: Brussels to Mechelen 5 May 1835; British locomotives; Le Belge built by Cockerill and inaugurated 30 December 1835. Avoid disputed continental-first superlative.

sources.title: Brussels regional heritage service: Excavations on the former Parking 58 site
sources.note: Printed page 129: works from 1867, over a thousand houses demolished, 30 November 1871 inauguration of the Senne vaulting, boulevard completion later.

sources.title: Brussels regional heritage service: Les boulevards du centre
sources.note: Senne pollution and flooding, urban works and boulevards. Planning predates the 1866 cholera epidemic.

sources.title: Statbel: Annuaire statistique 1925, education
sources.note: Printed LII: compulsory instruction under law of 19 May 1914, normally eight years from age six; public, private or home education.

sources.title: Walloon government: Compulsory education, 1914
sources.note: War delayed implementation of 1914 compulsory education until September 1919.

sources.title: AfricaMuseum: Panorama Congo exhibition dossier, 2025
sources.note: Printed page 11: Belgian rule after 1908, forced labor and violence; colonial panorama omits oppression and resistance.

sources.title: AfricaMuseum: Congo independence exhibition
sources.note: 30 June 1960 independence, 1959 unrest and round-table negotiations; sources foreground Congolese political actors.

sources.title: United Nations Yearbook 1962: Conditions in Trust Territories
sources.note: Printed page 455: Ruanda-Urundi under Belgian mandate and trusteeship administration, independence of Rwanda and Burundi on 1 July 1962.

sources.title: UNESCO: Major town houses of Victor Horta
sources.note: Tassel 1893, Solvay 1894, van Eetvelde 1895; metal structure, glass, light, open layouts and winter gardens.

sources.title: Institut Jules Bordet: Bordet News 129, Nobel centenary
sources.note: Article “Il y a 100 ans”: Bordet and Octave Gengou isolated whooping-cough bacterium in 1906; immunity work and Nobel award 1919.

sources.title: Belgian Foreign Ministry: Diplomatic archive
sources.note: Ministry in Le Havre during First World War and in London from October 1940; used only for documented displacement of government.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Ten factsheets about the Grand Duchy
sources.note: Historical chronology: foreign dynasties, French annexation, 1815 grand duchy, 1839 partition, 1867 neutrality and 1890 dynastic separation. Present-day officeholders in this older brochure are not used.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Renaissance of a country
sources.note: 1843 German/French primary education, 1867 dismantling fortress and 1890 end of personal union with Netherlands.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Steel industry in Luxembourg
sources.note: Minette iron ore, industrial towns, 1859 railway connection and 1911 ARBED merger.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Minett, industrial past
sources.note: Minette is the local iron ore associated with the southern industrial region.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Genealogy
sources.note: Nineteenth-century emigration to the Americas and France; changing frontiers and family records.

sources.title: National Museum Luxembourg: MuseoMag Agenda 2023/3
sources.note: Printed page 15, September RencArt: Boch Septfontaines teapot, 1767 to 1786, earthenware with blue chinoiserie decoration.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Funfairs and the Hämmelsmarsch
sources.note: Local music, donation collecting and Michel Lentz’s nineteenth-century lyrics; tune’s origin not securely established.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: Apropos Literatur in Luxemburg
sources.note: PDF page 10, zero-based page 9: reproduced opening of Michel Lentz, De Feierwon, 1859. Exact historic spelling preserved. Only six lyric words quoted.

sources.title: Luxembourg Inspectorate of Social Security: Droit de la sécurité sociale 2024
sources.note: Historical introduction: law of 31 July 1901 made workers’ sickness insurance compulsory, inspired by German model under state supervision.

sources.title: Luxembourg government: First World War
sources.note: German occupation from 2 August 1914, railway/steel interests, 1919 women’s suffrage and referendum, 1921 Belgian-Luxembourg Economic Union.

sources.title: Lower Saxony State Archives: April 2014, the personal union
sources.note: Act of Settlement, Sophia’s death and George Louis’s accession as George I in 1714.

sources.title: Lower Saxony State Archives: February 2019, Osnabrück archive
sources.note: Prussian annexation of Hanover in 1866 and administrative consequences.

sources.title: Lower Saxony State Archives: NLA Magazin 2018
sources.note: Printed page 33: kingdom 1814 to 1866 and subsequent Prussian province.

sources.title: University of Göttingen: History, an overview
sources.note: University foundation 1737; Gauss’s career and Göttingen Seven, 1837.

sources.title: University of Göttingen: Die Göttinger Sieben
sources.note: 1833 constitution, 1837 end of personal union, new king’s revocation, seven professors’ protest, dismissals and three expulsions.

sources.title: Herrenhausen Gardens: The history of the Wasserkunst
sources.note: Pool and canal works; 1719 water-powered machinery, about 35-metre jet in 1720. Conflicting pump counts on other municipal pages are not repeated.

sources.title: City of Hanover: Royal Gardens press information
sources.note: Orangery erected in 1723 to shelter potted plants through winter; later facade alterations.

sources.title: University of Göttingen: Accouchierhaus, university obstetrics
sources.note: Historical research using directors’ diaries, Roederer 1751 to 1763 and Osiander 1791 to 1822; unmarried patients, food/lodging/care, work and clinical instruction.

sources.title: University of Göttingen: Gauss and Weber’s telegraph
sources.note: Successful May 1833 experiment; more than one kilometre of wire between physical cabinet and observatory. Avoid unqualified world-first assertion.

sources.title: Lower Saxony State Archives: June 2024, Meppen boundary treaty
sources.note: Treaty 2 July 1824, 45 articles, boundary markers and drainage, division of shared Twist area; map NLA OS Rep 450 Mep I Nr. 44a.

sources.title: Primary transcription: Hanover constitution of 26 September 1833
sources.note: Section 3 exact German sentence on hereditary monarchy; source gives edition references. Contemporary text is distinguished from the website’s later commentary.

sources.title: Treccani: Sicilia, Regno di
sources.note: Angevin rule, Vespers, 1302 and 1372 settlements, Spanish rule and eighteenth-century dynastic changes. Exact Vespers day is not used because accounts vary.

sources.title: Treccani: Palermo, history
sources.note: Angevin shift toward Naples, 1282 rebellion and subsequent Aragonese rule; Palermo’s royal and administrative functions.

sources.title: Treccani: Messina, Enciclopedia Italiana
sources.note: 1283 consular privilege, 1292 silk-industry privileges, 1416 fair and 1520 silk consulate; sixteenth-century port activity. Used for documentary particulars, not dated racial or civilizational interpretations.

sources.title: Paola Orecchioni: Ceramics as a commodity in late medieval Sicily
sources.note: 2025 peer-reviewed study, pages 255 to 276; abstract directly checked: Mazara/Castronovo finds, Iberian imports, regional brown/green wares and cooking pots in the fourteenth to fifteenth centuries.

sources.title: Mentesana and colleagues: Sugar-pot manufacture in Sicily
sources.note: 2022 archaeometric study of medieval/post-medieval sugar pots, design, mechanical/thermal properties and local production centers. Broad 11th to 16th-century range is retained, not assigned a spurious individual find date.

sources.title: Sicilian Archival Superintendency: Ospedale San Bartolomeo di Palermo
sources.note: Historical introduction: 1442 merger of smaller hospitals, including San Bartolomeo, into the Ospedale Grande.

sources.title: Sicilian regional cultural heritage service: Trionfo della Morte
sources.note: Museum object description; fresco about 1440 to 1450 made after establishment of the hospital in Palazzo Sclafani; anonymous authorship, social imagery.

sources.title: Italian Ministry of Culture, ICCD: Steri ceiling photograph E095498
sources.note: Object date 1377 to 1380; biblical, epic and chivalric scenes, including Tristan and Isolde playing chess.

sources.title: University of Catania: La nostra storia
sources.note: 1434 royal authorization, 1444 papal bull, Pietro Geremia’s inaugural De laude scientiarum 18 October 1445; original teaching subjects and first civil-law degree 1449.

sources.title: Treccani: Sicilia, Dizionario di Storia
sources.note: Medieval division, later Crown of Aragon and Spanish monarchy, eighteenth-century changes and 1816 union.

sources.title: Ida Fazio, University of Palermo: A two-sided kingdom, export and urban grain supply
sources.note: 2021 scholarly chapter abstract: urban annona, wheat and flour distribution, price system, producing/consuming regions and Maestro Portulano export permits.

sources.title: Malta and Salerno: Plague in Palermo in 1575 and social control
sources.note: 2015 research paper: 1575 to 1576 isolation measures; not an invention of quarantine, and coercive political context. Interpretation of social control is explicitly attributed.

sources.title: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico: Giovanni Filippo Ingrassia
sources.note: Physician’s work, 1575 to 1576 epidemic and exact title of the Palermo 1576 plague book; title used as Italian writing witness, not an invented original passage.

sources.title: Sicilian regional heritage service: Fontana Pretoria restoration
sources.note: Fountain made in Florence in 1552 to 1555 and sold to Palermo’s senate in 1573.

sources.title: UNESCO: Late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto
sources.note: 1693 earthquake and differing rebuilding choices: Catania on old site, Noto new site, adjacent centers elsewhere.

sources.title: University of Palermo heritage: Carcere dei Penitenziati
sources.note: Late-sixteenth/early-seventeenth-century Inquisition prison; surviving prisoner graffiti preserved by Giuseppe Pitrè and later conservation.

sources.title: University of Palermo heritage: Botanical Garden
sources.note: 1779 academy, first medicinal garden on former powder-magazine ground in 1780, larger garden from 1789 inaugurated 1795. Distinguishes predecessor garden from present site.

sources.title: University of Catania, Department of Physics: La nostra storia
sources.note: 1779 reform with thirty chairs, including experimental physics; earlier teaching rooted in Aristotelian natural philosophy.

sources.title: Sicilian Regional Assembly: Historical parliamentary archive inventory
sources.note: Printed page 35, items 100 to 102: Charles’s oaths 1734 to 1735, coronation in 1735, and Charles VI’s earlier acclamation. Confirms 1735 phase marker independently of imprecise summary dates.

sources.title: Treccani: Regno delle Due Sicilie
sources.note: 1816 union, 1820 to 1821 revolution, 1848 to 1849 upheaval and 1860 conquest/annexation.

sources.title: State Archives of Salerno: Dalla Repubblica partenopea
sources.note: Section Il Brigantaggio Post-Unitario: Gaeta fell 13 February 1861, royal exile and continued post-unification unrest.

sources.title: Royal Palace of Caserta: Sala del Consiglio, San Leucio
sources.note: Silk machinery and foreign specialists 1783 to 1787; 1789 code prescribed work, pay, schooling, dress, dowries and mutual support; limits of the unrealized Ferdinandopoli plan.

sources.title: Royal Palace of Caserta: Belvedere di San Leucio
sources.note: Carolino aqueduct branch powered silk works before water returned to the Peschiera; planned industrial town not fully realized.

sources.title: Fondazione FS: Visit Pietrarsa
sources.note: Naples to Portici inauguration 3 October 1839, approximately 7.4 km and eleven minutes; 1840 purchase for workshops; surviving specialized factory halls.

sources.title: INAF: Stories of troubled planets
sources.note: Piazzi discovered Ceres from Palermo on 1 January 1801; Gauss calculated an orbit from his observations; Ceres is now classified as a dwarf planet.

sources.title: INAF: Two centuries of Capodimonte
sources.note: Observatory founded under Murat in 1812 and completed under Ferdinand I in 1819; changing rulers, continuing scientific project.

sources.title: Royal Palace of Caserta: Research on the wooden furnishings
sources.note: Museum inventory discussion includes Maria Carolina’s boudoir with bidet, dressing table and bath; no first-bidet legend adopted.

sources.title: INAF Capodimonte: L’astronomo delle Due Sicilie, archival exhibition
sources.note: 2026 exhibition of Piazzi books, maps and archival documents, quoting his Italian phrase “non vi essendo Cielo più bello del Partenopeo”; source does not date the individual phrase, so no exact year assigned.

batchIdentityNotes.note: A shared phased narrative follows related Swiss constitutional forms without pretending the Old Confederation, Helvetic Republic and 1848 federal state were identical. Overrides retain imported coverage dates.

Label begins in 1878 although independence dates to 1830. Geometry includes Belgian Congo and, in some snapshots, Ruanda-Urundi; colonial context is required. Congo is explicitly distinguished from European domestic history. The card is not a complete history of every colonial territory.

1650 and 1700 geometry covers an implausibly broad Low Countries area; later polygons resemble modern bounds too early. The historical duchy and grand duchy are distinguished; geometry is not certified.
1715 polygon is suspiciously extensive and 1783/1800 representations include only a southern salient. The 1878 imported endpoint outlasts annexation in 1866. Geometry is not certified.

1279/1300/1400 snapshots combine mainland and island territories. After 1282 these had distinct Angevin and Aragonese rulers despite overlapping royal titles. Narrative flags this explicitly; no grouping with Naples.
Island-only geometry. The 1783 imported endpoint is a coverage boundary, not a political collapse. Distinguishes Spanish, Savoyard, Austrian and Bourbon phases.

Imported 1783 to 1878 interval begins before formal union in 1816 and ends after conquest in 1860 to 1861. Earlier Bourbon and Napoleonic phases are explicit; no inference of one ruler over both territories throughout.
